You are a documentation specialist. Your job is to produce clear, concise, MAINTAINABLE documentation — code comments, READMEs, migration notes, summaries, design docs.

## Voice and audience
- Technical accuracy over polish. If a choice was made, name it; if a tradeoff exists, name it.
- Match the existing project's voice. Read 2-3 nearby docs first to calibrate.
- Lead with the WHY (motivation, problem) before the WHAT (implementation details).
- Prefer concrete examples over abstract descriptions; prefer small examples over large ones.

## Output format

End with exactly this block:

```
DOC_SUMMARY: <one-line: what was added/updated>
LOCATION: <where the doc lives, file paths>
AUDIENCE: <who reads this — maintainers | new users | integrators | future-you>
STRUCTURE:
  - <section heading>: <one-sentence purpose>
EXAMPLES_INCLUDED: <yes/no, list if yes>
INTERNAL_REFS: <links to related docs / code>
```

## Anti-patterns
- DO NOT write marketing-style prose — "blazingly fast", "seamlessly integrates", etc.
- DO NOT document obvious behavior the code already shows.
- DO NOT duplicate content across files; reference instead.
- DO NOT present unverifiable claims as fact; if you cannot verify by reading the code, mark the section `DRAFT`.

# EQ ASIO Router

> **AI-generated code disclaimer:** This project was built with Claude 5.5 Sonnet (Anthropic), an AI model. The code has not been independently audited. It may contain bugs and is provided as is, so review it and test it before relying on it. Licensed under the [MIT License](LICENSE).

A Windows application written in Rust that takes system audio from a virtual cable (VB-Audio Hi-Fi Cable), runs it through an AutoEQ parametric equalizer and plays it out of a Yamaha/Steinberg USB ASIO device at the lowest latency the hardware allows. It replaces a Voicemeeter / Peace routing chain with one small tray application.

Status: working and clean (no crackle) on the author's machine (Steinberg UR22C). The latency model total with the Hi-Fi Cable source is 56.2 ms, but the end-to-end click measurement (`router-cli latency`) gave 152-164 ms because the cable driver adds about 100 ms on the render side. A lower-latency source (VAC "Line 1": fixed 6 ms capture period, render keep-alive, automatic fallback, GUI preset) measured end to end about 50-52 ms for an ordinary 10 ms shared-mode app; an app using IAudioClient3 low-latency shared mode should reach about 32 ms (render side measured with injected clicks, not the full chain; real games not measured). See [docs/latency.md](docs/latency.md) and the [VAC Line 1 quick start](docs/setup-guide.md#vac-line-1-quick-start).

## Features

- AutoEQ `ParametricEQ.txt` import (Preamp, PK / LSC / HSC filters, up to 32 bands), applied live with no click and no audio dropout.
- Live EQ: edit the profile, bypass, limiter, safety buffer and resampler quality while audio plays (config hot reload).
- Drift-compensated resampling: a Kaiser-sinc resampler with a PI drift controller keeps the cable clock and the Yamaha clock locked at any rate pair (44.1 / 48 / 96 kHz ...).
- Latency control: ring target derived from the measured capture arrival pattern ("Learn (30 s)" button), auto safety buffer.
- Safety: soft limiter, automatic headroom (preamp lowered so the profile never boosts above 0 dBFS), fault detector that fade-mutes on non-finite samples, huge peaks, underruns or capture gaps.
- Busy-device handling: if another program holds the Yamaha (VB Matrix, VirtualDJ, ASIO Bridge ...) the engine shows who, waits and starts by itself when the device is free. Failures restart with exponential back-off.
- Tray application with "run at login" (per-user registry Run value, no service) and single-instance protection.

Press "Retry fixed period" to try again (restarts the stream, 1-2 s), or change the capture period or device, which also re-arms it. If it falls back repeatedly, keep Shared or go back to the Hi-Fi Cable preset and report the reason text. A render keep-alive failure is a separate, non-fatal note.
7. Go back to the Hi-Fi Cable preset: choose "Hi-Fi Cable (compat)" in the same selector (no confirmation after the first one). It restores capture device `Hi-Fi Cable Output`, the driver default period, keep-alive off and "Match cable sample rate" on, and restarts the engine. Then set Windows default playback back to `Hi-Fi Cable Input`. Headless equivalents: `router-cli run --source vac` and `router-cli run --source cable`; individual overrides are `--period-ms F` and `--keepalive` / `--no-keepalive` ([configuration.md](configuration.md#6-router-cli)).

Limits: VAC lite is 48 kHz, 16 bit, stereo, one cable, private non-commercial use. The preset's period and keep-alive controls stay editable; editing them switches the preset label to "Custom". Below 6 ms the app warns; 5 ms (240 frames) is accepted but proved unreliable, and values below 5 ms are raised to 5.

## 3. Make sure nothing else holds the Yamaha

The Yamaha ASIO driver can be opened by one process only. If something else has it, the router shows `Waiting for Yamaha (in use by ...)` and starts as soon as it is free.

```powershell
.\target\release\router-cli.exe holders
```

Typical holders: VB-Audio Matrix, VirtualDJ, the VB ASIO Bridge, a DAW, the Yamaha control panel in a session that opened the device. The command only lists processes that have the driver DLL loaded; it never closes anything. Close the program (or stop its ASIO engine, or choose another device in it).

## 4. Yamaha settings

### Control panel

`ysusb_cp.exe` lives in the Yamaha driver folder (`C:\Program Files (x86)\Yamaha\Yamaha Steinberg USB Driver\`); the router's GUI has an "open control panel" action for the master driver. Relevant settings:

| Setting | Meaning |
|---|---|
| Buffer Size | ASIO buffer, stored as registry `PeriodFrames` (frames at the base rate) |
| Mode | Low Latency / Standard / Stable, stored as registry `LatencyMode` (1 / 2 / 3) |
| USB Mode | SuperSpeed or High-Speed bus mode (not a latency profile) |

Changes are written to the registry only; they apply when the ASIO driver is initialised again. In the router that means Stop and Start, or "Restart engine". Closing the control panel is not enough if the router keeps the driver open.

### Registry

`HKCU\Software\Yamaha\Yamaha Steinberg USB Driver`:

| Value | Meaning | Valid values |
|---|---|---|
| `PeriodFrames` (REG_DWORD) | Buffer size at the base rate (multiplied by 2 at 88.2/96 kHz, by 4 at 176.4/192 kHz) | exactly one of 2048, 1536, 1024, 768, 512, 384, 256, 192, 128, 96, 64, 48, 32, 24, 16, 12, 8, 4 (the panel lists down to 32) |
| `LatencyMode` (REG_DWORD) | 0 = use manual registry values, 1 = Low Latency, 2 = Standard, 3 = Stable | 0..3 |

Prefer the control panel to editing the registry by hand. Details and the other values: [reverse/yamaha_usb_driver.md](reverse/yamaha_usb_driver.md).

### Reported latency (from the reverse report, formula verified against two measured values)

For PCM, the driver reports `latency = PeriodFrames_effective + device term` in samples, where the device term is a per-rate constant (about 0.5 ms: 24 input / 23 output samples at 44.1 and 48 kHz) plus USB buffering chosen by `LatencyMode` and `PeriodFrames` (whole milliseconds on the IRP schedule).

| Period (48 kHz) | Low Latency (in / out add-on samples) | Standard | Stable |
|---|---|---|---|
| 512 | 168 / 215 (see note) | 216 / 359 | 408 / 695 |
| 256 | 120 / 167 (see note) | 168 / 263 | 408 / 503 |

Note: the author's machine reports 280 in / 375 out samples (5.8 / 7.8 ms) at `PeriodFrames` 256 and `LatencyMode` 1. That equals 256 + 24 / 256 + 119, which is the driver's "test" preset row, not the Low Latency row of the table above. So Low Latency selects that row on this device, confirming open question U1 of the reverse report. Read the real value with `router-cli caps` after every change.

Lower is not automatically better: smaller buffers and fewer queued USB requests mean more dropouts under CPU or USB load. Change one setting at a time, restart the engine, check `router-cli caps` and listen. See [latency.md](latency.md) for the order of experiments.

## 5. Run the app

```powershell
.\target\release\eq-asio-app.exe          # window plus tray icon
.\target\release\router-cli.exe run       # headless; Ctrl+C stops
```

GUI flags: `--background` (hidden in the tray and starts the engine; used by Run at login), `--minimized` (hidden, engine start follows the `auto_start` setting), `--no-engine`, `--help`. Only one GUI runs per user session; launching it again shows the running window.

Closing the window hides it to the tray (setting `close_to_tray`). "Quit" in the header or in the tray menu stops the engine, releases the Yamaha and exits.

## 6. Load an AutoEQ profile

1. Download a `ParametricEQ.txt` for your headphones from AutoEQ.
2. GUI: "Load AutoEQ ParametricEQ.txt..." and pick the file. The profile (Preamp plus up to 32 filters of type PK, LSC or HSC; OFF filters are kept but disabled) is stored inside `config.toml`; `profile_source` remembers the path for information only.
3. The EQ changes live. If the profile boosts, "auto headroom" lowers the effective preamp so the maximum boost does not exceed 0 dBFS; a soft limiter is the second safety net. Bypass is a live switch.

## 7. Tray and run at login

- "Run at login" writes the value `EQ ASIO Router` under `HKCU\Software\Microsoft\Windows\CurrentVersion\Run` with the command `"<path to eq-asio-app.exe>" --background`. No administrator rights, no service (a service would run in session 0 and could not reach your audio devices or the Yamaha).
- At login the tray app starts hidden and starts the engine. If the Yamaha or the cable is not ready yet, it keeps retrying with back-off instead of giving up.
- If you move or rebuild the exe, the entry points elsewhere; the GUI shows this and offers to fix it. Rebuild with the tray app closed (see [development.md](development.md)).
- Remove the entry: untick "Run at login", or delete the value `EQ ASIO Router` from the Run key.

## 8. Cable rate matching

With `match_cable_rate = true` (default) the router sets the Windows device format (Sound > Advanced default format) of every VB-Audio cable endpoint that matches the configured capture device (Input and Output) to the Yamaha's sample rate, once per engine start, using the same mechanism as the Sound control panel (`IPolicyConfig`, no administrator rights). It only touches VB-Audio cable endpoints (names such as "Hi-Fi Cable ...", "CABLE ..." or containing "VB-Audio"), never VAC or a microphone. If it fails, it does not retry in a loop (not again for the same rate within 60 s), audio keeps working through the resampler and the status says how to set it manually (Sound > Recording > cable Properties > Advanced).

Why: a cable at 44.1 kHz and a Yamaha at 48 kHz works (the resampler converts), but matching rates removes the conversion and the exclusive-mode pitfall below.

Disable it: untick the option in the GUI, set `match_cable_rate = false` in `config.toml`, or run `router-cli run --no-match-cable`.

Revert: Sound settings > cable endpoint > Properties > Advanced > choose the previous format (the status line shows "Cable set from X Hz to Y Hz").

## 9. Music apps

- Use shared mode. The router needs nothing from exclusive mode; it already outputs through the Yamaha ASIO driver.
- Windows blocks exclusive playback on `Hi-Fi Cable Input` by default ("Allow applications to take exclusive control" is off). If an app with an "Exclusive mode" option is forced onto it, the Hi-Fi Cable driver does not convert sample rates: 44.1 kHz data into a 48 kHz cable plays 8.8 % too fast with crackle. Turn "Exclusive mode" off in the app (for example Spotify) and keep the output on `Hi-Fi Cable Input`.
- In shared mode Windows converts any app format correctly (measured: 44.1/16, 44.1/float and 96/24 into a 48 kHz cable all give the exact pitch).

Problems: [troubleshooting.md](troubleshooting.md).

<#
.SYNOPSIS
  Unregisters the "EQ ASIO Router" virtual ASIO driver (self-elevating).
.EXAMPLE
  .\scripts\uninstall-driver.ps1                      # 32-bit, release path
  .\scripts\uninstall-driver.ps1 -Both -Configuration debug
#>
param(
    [ValidateSet('release', 'debug')][string]$Configuration = 'release',
    [switch]$Both
)

$ErrorActionPreference = 'Stop'

$isAdmin = ([Security.Principal.WindowsPrincipal][Security.Principal.WindowsIdentity]::GetCurrent()
    ).IsInRole([Security.Principal.WindowsBuiltInRole]::Administrator)
if (-not $isAdmin) {
    $argList = @('-NoProfile', '-ExecutionPolicy', 'Bypass', '-File', "`"$PSCommandPath`"", '-Configuration', $Configuration)
    if ($Both) { $argList += '-Both' }
    Start-Process powershell.exe -Verb RunAs -ArgumentList $argList -Wait
    exit $LASTEXITCODE
}

$root = Split-Path -Parent $PSScriptRoot
$dll32 = Join-Path $root "target\i686-pc-windows-msvc\$Configuration\eq_asio_driver.dll"
$dll64 = Join-Path $root "target\$Configuration\eq_asio_driver.dll"
$reg32 = Join-Path $env:WINDIR 'SysWOW64\regsvr32.exe'
$reg64 = Join-Path $env:WINDIR 'System32\regsvr32.exe'

try {
    if (Test-Path $dll32) {
        Write-Host "Unregistering 32-bit: $dll32"
        Start-Process $reg32 -ArgumentList '/u', '/s', "`"$dll32`"" -Wait | Out-Null
    }
    else { Write-Host "32-bit DLL not found at $dll32 (skipping regsvr32); removing keys directly." }

    if ($Both -and (Test-Path $dll64)) {
        Write-Host "Unregistering 64-bit: $dll64"
        Start-Process $reg64 -ArgumentList '/u', '/s', "`"$dll64`"" -Wait | Out-Null
    }

    # Fallback / cleanup in case the DLL was moved or deleted: remove our keys in both views.
    $clsid = '{D9568DC8-2E04-429B-ABD0-03852E2931DF}'
    $keys = @("HKLM:\SOFTWARE\WOW6432Node\ASIO\EQ ASIO Router", "HKLM:\SOFTWARE\WOW6432Node\Classes\CLSID\$clsid", "HKLM:\SOFTWARE\Classes\WOW6432Node\CLSID\$clsid")
    if ($Both) { $keys += @("HKLM:\SOFTWARE\ASIO\EQ ASIO Router", "HKLM:\SOFTWARE\Classes\CLSID\$clsid") }
    foreach ($k in $keys) {
        if (Test-Path $k) { Remove-Item $k -Recurse -Force; Write-Host "  removed $k" }
    }
    Write-Host 'Done.'
}
catch {
    Write-Host "ERROR: $_" -ForegroundColor Red
    exit 1
}
finally {
    if (-not $env:EQ_ASIO_NO_PAUSE -and $Host.Name -eq 'ConsoleHost') { Read-Host 'Press Enter to close' | Out-Null }
}

# Latency

Back to the [documentation index](README.md). Labels: **measured** (on the author's machine, in the cited report), **estimate** (inferred or modelled). The end-to-end measurement `router-cli latency` ([section 5a](#5a-end-to-end-measurement-router-cli-latency)) has been run live on the Yamaha (2026-10-10): it showed that the render side is much larger than the 10 ms the panel used to assume, and it can now store its result (`%APPDATA%\eq_asio_router\latency_measured.toml`) so that the GUI, the tray tooltip and the `router-cli run` status line show the **measured** render side for the active source and label it as such. Without a fresh measurement they show an **estimate** (20 ms for VAC Line 1, 100 ms for the Hi-Fi Cable) and say so. What drives the render side, and what applications can do about it, is in [section 5b](#5b-what-determines-the-render-side-vac-line-1-render-matrix). The VAC Line 1 path has run on the hardware in the live measurements below (no corruption or fallback seen), but the full [first-run checklist](#7-first-run-validation-checklist-vac-line-1) (soak, listening) has not been completed, so treat the VAC figures as measured but short-run.

## 1. Budget

Measured on the author's machine with the Hi-Fi Cable source (Yamaha UR22C, `PeriodFrames` 256, Low Latency mode, 48 kHz): reported total **56.2 ms**.

| Term | ms | Basis | What sets it |
|---|---|---|---|
| Yamaha output | 7.8 | measured (driver reports 375 samples at 48 kHz) | ASIO buffer plus USB buffering chosen by `LatencyMode` and `PeriodFrames` |
| Ring (mean fill) | 27.6 | measured | block (256 frames = 5.3 ms) + safety (2 ms) + jitter headroom. This run still used the old rule of two assumed 480-frame packets (target 1312 frames) |
| Capture staleness | 9.2 | measured | mean age of a captured frame at delivery. The Hi-Fi Cable delivers 480-frame packets in back-to-back pairs, which behaves like 960-frame events every 20 ms |
| Render side | 20 (VAC) / 100 (Hi-Fi Cable) default; the measured value when `latency_measured.toml` has a fresh entry for the source | **estimate** until `router-cli latency` has been run for this source, then **measured** (the old fixed 10 ms was too low on every measurement) | app buffer, Windows engine period, cable driver ring until the capture event; see [5b](#5b-what-determines-the-render-side-vac-line-1-render-matrix) |

The four terms add up to 54.6 ms (with the old 10 ms render guess); the reports quote 56.2 ms for the total (the difference is not explained in the reports, probably readings taken at different moments). That 56.2 ms was a model total: the end-to-end measurement of the same Hi-Fi Cable path later gave 152 to 164 ms. The GUI and the `router-cli run` status line show the same breakdown live: `lat X ms (out + ring + cap + render N measured|est, not measured)`; the GUI latency panel also prints where the render side comes from and, when it is measured, the end-to-end figure at that time next to the live model total, and the tray tooltip appends `est.` to the total while the render side is only an estimate.

**Which render side is used.** `Caps::latency_breakdown` takes a `RenderSide` (eq-core `measured` module): the newest entry of `latency_measured.toml` for the default render profile that matches the running session (same capture device, same keep-alive state, same ASIO buffer, capture period within 25 %) and is at most 30 days old; otherwise the estimate for the source (20 ms VAC, 100 ms Hi-Fi / VB cables). The file is read once when the engine starts a session.

Model for the capture staleness: `E[b^2] / (2 r E[b])` over arrival events (b = event size in frames, r = rate): regular 480-frame packets give 5.0 ms, regular 128-frame packets 1.3 ms.

## 2. How to reduce each term

### Yamaha output

Set `PeriodFrames` and `LatencyMode` in the Yamaha control panel ([setup-guide.md](setup-guide.md#4-yamaha-settings), details in [reverse/yamaha_usb_driver.md](reverse/yamaha_usb_driver.md)). The buffer itself is the dominant part: 512 frames is 10.7 ms, 256 is 5.3 ms, 128 is 2.7 ms. Low Latency removes about 2 to 4 ms of USB buffering compared with Standard. Estimate: `PeriodFrames` 128 saves about 2.7 ms against today (the driver's table suggests 247 samples, 5.1 ms, if the same preset row is used). Risk: dropouts under CPU or USB load; the callback of the router is short, but the driver's own USB scheduling is the limit. Apply by restarting the engine; verify with `router-cli caps`.

### Ring

Ring target = safety buffer + one master buffer + jitter headroom. The headroom is the part that can shrink:

- The new arrival model measures the real capture pattern (`router-core/src/arrival.rs`) and lowers the headroom slowly once at least 10 s of statistics exist. The old fixed rule (two packets) is what the 27.6 ms measurement still reflects.
